submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective lexical detector at layer 1: the pole fires on the current token when that token is a nominal of the 'listed item / reported quantity' family - plural count nouns and -tion/-ment/-er/-ity/-ship nominalizations such as ' bodies', ' names', ' sources', ' factors', ' documents', ' folders', ' statements', ' agencies', ' countries', ' cases' or ' results' (peak 0.2-1.4), and more weakly on singular abstract nouns such as ' health', ' life', ' case', ' proof' or ' world'. It sits at the GELU floor (about -0.17) on function words, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, punctuation, animal names and occupational-role nouns, and its membership is lexical rather than purely semantic, so near-synonyms split (' names' much greater than ' tags', ' factors' greater than ' reasons', ' bodies' greater than ' corpses'); strength is graded and dips in a text's first few positions (at position 0 it is active on every token, hence the first-token floor).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The county archive had occupied the same brick building since the nineteen thirties, and for most of that time nobody had thought very hard about what was inside it. The cellar smelled of dust and old paper, and the shelving ran in a long row from the door to the back wall. In winter the radiator clanked and the window fogged, and in summer the cellar was cool enough that the staff took their lunch down there. A clerk named Martha had worked there for a quarter of a century, and she could find almost anything a visitor asked for, though she often did so slowly and with a great deal of sighing. When the county announced that the building would be sold, Martha was the first to object. She wrote a letter to the board, then another, and then a third, each longer and angrier than the last. The board did not reply. So she began to take an inventory of what the office held, working along the shelving one bay at a time, and the longer she worked the more surprised she became. There was a ledger from the eighteen nineties recording the sale of farmland, and a bundle of old mail from a family who had moved west and then, a decade later, written back to ask about a deed. There was a map of a river that no longer ran where the map said it ran, and a photograph of a main street that had burned down twice, and a shoebox holding what a schoolteacher had written to a soldier who never came home. Martha typed a summary of what she found and sent it to the board, and this time somebody read it. A reporter came out from the paper, then a historian from the state college, then a young man from the heritage trust who talked very fast and took a photograph of everything. Within a month the sale had been postponed, and within a year the building had been named a landmark, which meant that the roof would be repaired and the cellar would be dried out and the shelving would stay where it was. Martha was asked to give a tour on the day the plaque went up. She stood at the top of the stair and talked about the river, the fire, the mail, and the schoolteacher, and the visitor listened and asked a question and took a note. Afterwards a woman from the trust thanked her and said that it was wonderful how much history had been saved, and Martha said that it had not been saved, it had merely been sitting there, and that the difference mattered. The woman laughed, not unkindly, and went to look at the map. By the time the building closed for the evening, Martha had shown the documents to a visitor from the trust and had answered the same question a second time, and the visitor had written down every word.
